mcqs.question: Why is a retailer's steady-state checkout rate a poor guide for sizing a flash-sale launch?
options: A flash sale concentrates a huge multiple of normal attempt volume onto a tiny slice of inventory, unlike steady-state traffic spread across many SKUs
Steady-state traffic always uses a different payment provider than flash-sale traffic
Flash sales only affect the shipping service, not checkout itself
Steady-state checkout never touches the inventory service at all
mcqs.explanation: A flash sale isn't just "more traffic" — it's the same shape of problem as a ticket on-sale: massive concurrent demand narrowed onto one or a few hot SKUs, which is a contention problem the average daily rate says nothing about. The other options describe things not actually true of steady-state checkout.

mcqs.question: Why model checkout as a saga instead of a single order row that flips from pending to confirmed?
options: A single-row model can't store a payment token
There's no automatic cross-service rollback if a later step fails, so the saga must track exactly how far it got to know which compensating actions to run
Sagas are a PCI compliance requirement for all payment flows
A single row can't be indexed by customer ID
mcqs.explanation: Because inventory, payment, and shipping are separate services with no shared transaction, nothing automatically undoes an earlier step if a later one fails — the saga's whole purpose is tracking progress precisely enough to trigger the right compensations. The other options aren't real constraints here.

mcqs.question: Why must the idempotency-key record live in shared, durable storage rather than one server's local memory?
options: In-memory storage is always slower to read than a database
Idempotency keys must be encrypted at rest for compliance reasons
A retry can land on a different server instance than the original request, and it still needs to see the same recorded outcome
Compensating actions are stored in memory, so the key format has to match
mcqs.explanation: A retry after a timeout has no guarantee of hitting the same server — a load balancer can route it anywhere — so the record of "this key already completed with this outcome" has to be visible from any instance, which means shared durable storage, not local memory. The other reasons aren't why this constraint exists.

mcqs.question: What combination mitigates contention on a single hot SKU during a flash sale?
options: Charging every request's card first, to filter out non-serious buyers before touching inventory
Sharding the inventory row across multiple replicas that each hold a partial count
Increasing the payment provider's timeout so more requests can complete
An atomic conditional decrement on the inventory row, plus an admission-controlled queue that caps the write rate during the spike
mcqs.explanation: This mirrors ticket booking's hot-seat problem exactly: a conditional write lets the database arbitrate the race safely, while an admission-controlled queue shapes the arrival rate so the write volume stays sustainable. Charging first is the pitfall covered elsewhere, and sharding a single row's count doesn't solve exact-count correctness.

mcqs.question: What's the practical risk of charging payment before confirming an inventory reservation?
options: It always violates PCI-DSS regulations regardless of order
A successful charge followed by a failed inventory reservation forces a refund for a customer with no product — at flash-sale scale, that's a refund storm, not a rare edge case
Payment providers technically reject any charge attempted before an inventory check
It makes generating an idempotency key impossible
mcqs.explanation: Ordering payment before inventory means every lost inventory race after a successful charge becomes a refund — at flash-sale volume, that's a large fraction of a spike's traffic, not a rare failure. There's no such PCI rule or payment-provider rejection tied to ordering, and idempotency keys are independent of this.
